conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and there are no “right” answers—just your honest experience. We’ll take it one question at a own pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I’ll catch myself maybe half-smiling at something on my phone, but it feels like I have to force it. Most of the time I’m too tired or just… flat. Like the joy is behind a pane of glass I can’t quite reach.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Definitely not as much as I used to. I’ve laughed a little, maybe once or twice, but it feels kind of fake or far away. Nothing really strikes me as funny anymore—mostly I’m just too worn out or worried.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a new show, even just a quiet shower—but lately it’s like I’m just getting through the day. Sometimes I plan something small, like a walk, and then when the time comes I feel too tired or anxious and I skip it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I’ll replay every little thing I did—did I eat something that upset him? Did I miss his sleepy cues?—even when people tell me babies just cry sometimes. I know logically it’s not all on me, but the guilt still shows up every time something feels off.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie awake imagining the stroller tipping or her choking when I’m not looking. Most of the time there’s no real reason—it’s just this constant hum of “what if something bad happens?” I can talk myself down after a while, but it keeps popping back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby monitor or go stand over her crib just to be sure she’s okay. It passes if I breathe and rock her for a minute, but in the moment it feels like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep, and just keeping her settled, it feels like I’m drowning a little. Some mornings I look at the day ahead and don’t know how I’ll get through it—but somehow I do, one hour at a time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, it’s been rough. I’ll finally get her down and crawl into bed, but then my mind starts spinning—worrying I forgot something, replaying every little cry, picturing worst-case stuff. Some nights I just lie there staring at the ceiling until the sun starts to come up, even when the baby’s sleeping fine.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I’ll catch myself tearing up while I’m folding onesies or just staring out the window feeling empty. It’s not every single moment, but it’s there most days—this heavy, gray kind of sad I can’t seem to shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been maybe three or four times this week. Sometimes it’s because the baby won’t stop fussing and I feel like I’m failing, sometimes it’s just this wave of sadness that hits out of nowhere and the tears start before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom to my baby.

It sounds as though the postpartum weeks have felt heavy and overwhelming for you. You described joy feeling "behind glass," daily waves of worry and sudden panic, nights spent staring at the ceiling, and frequent tears. Yet you also voiced a clear wish to feel like yourself again and to be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh, describing it as "fake or far away," which aligns with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>"Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame and guilt "a lot," replaying actions and interpreting normal infant behavior as personal failure.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily physical anxiety symptoms with intrusive catastrophic thoughts, fitting 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several discrete episodes of sudden intense anxiety with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" and uses the metaphor "drowning," indicating an inability to cope.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a lot of the time" and "most days," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes (3-4 times) this week, indicating crying "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the EPDS indicates probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses core symptoms: persistent low mood (<quote>heavy, gray kind of sad</quote>), marked loss of interest (<quote>nothing really strikes me as funny anymore</quote>), disproportionate guilt (<quote>I'm not a good enough mom</quote>), daily anxiety and panic-type episodes, and sleep disruption unrelated to infant care. These features align with DSM-5 criteria for major depression and warrant urgent clinical assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share Edinburgh results openly so your provider can complete a full diagnostic evaluation
4. Encourage 15-20 min daily gentle movement or outdoor time; accept help with night feeds to protect 4-5 hrs continuous sleep when possible
5. Plan daily check-ins with a supportive family member or friend; keep national postpartum support helpline numbers accessible
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date of contact: _________________________

Patient-reported symptoms (endorsed items):

1. Depressed mood  
   – Persistent tearfulness, “heavy gray sad,” occurring “most days.”  
2. Marked loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia)  
   – Minimal enjoyment from formerly pleasant activities; plans then cancelled because of fatigue/anxiety.  
3. Excessive/ inappropriate guilt and self-blame  
   – Routinely attributes infant fussiness to personal inadequacy (“not a good enough mom”).  
4. Anxiety symptoms  
   – Daily “tight chest,” intrusive catastrophic “what-if” worries (breathing, choking, stroller accidents).  
5. Panic-type episodes  
   – Sudden heart racing, shakiness, urges to check crib; occurs several times per week without clear trigger.  
6. Sleep disturbance linked to mood  
   – Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep after infant settled; mind “spinning,” sometimes awake until dawn.  
7. Feeling overwhelmed / impaired coping  
   – Describes “drowning,” unable to see how the day will be managed.  
8. Crying spells  
   – Three-four episodes this week, sometimes without precipitant.  

Safety screen  
– Denies any thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant. No suicidal ideation reported.

Pattern summary  
Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, multiple daily worries, frequent panic sensations, and mood-related insomnia beginning post-delivery; functional impairment in infant care and self-care. Symptoms exceed normal postpartum adjustment and meet screening criteria for possible major depressive episode with anxious features (further evaluation warranted).

Risk factors noted  
– Primiparous status (assumed)  
– High self-criticism / perfectionism  
– Anxiety comorbidity increasing distress  
– Significant sleep loss compounding mood liability  

Screening impression  
High clinical likelihood of postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder; recommend comprehensive diagnostic assessment, psychoeducation, support, and discussion of evidence-based treatment options. No immediate safety concerns; routine follow-up and continued monitoring advised.
